w: What's tested Sertoli cells versus Leydig cells: where each sits, which gonadotropin drives it, what it makes and what it feeds back on (he said this is where he would study) The 4 G's of sexual differentiation, and how the testes and their hormones (AMH, testosterone and DHT) build a male; androgen insensitivity syndrome and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency How the testis is organized, and how spermatogenesis, spermiation and maturation in the epididymis happen; keeping the testes at 34 degrees Celsius Testosterone synthesis and metabolism: LH and cholesterol desmolase, aromatase (mostly in the Sertoli cells) and 5-alpha-reductase Control by the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis: GnRH, LH, FSH, inhibin and testosterone feedback, and reading a hormone pattern The accessory glands, what each adds to semen, and the semen clot Autonomic control of erection and ejaculation ("point and shoot"), and how sildenafil works Dr. Matthew Madison, PhD, of the Department of Medicine (Division of Pulmonary, Allergy and Critical Care Medicine), gave this lecture on Friday, November 6; his slides title it "Male Reproductive Endocrinology." He told the class he inherited the lecture. These notes follow his recorded lecture and his slides. He comes back on Tuesday, November 10, for the female reproductive tract and pregnancy (L16 and L17), and he gives the Exam 2 review on Wednesday, November 11. What he stressed: comparing and contrasting Sertoli and Leydig cells ("this is where I would study"), AMH and the Müllerian ducts ("an important piece to remember"), Leydig cells as the testosterone makers ("worth remembering"), which feedback hormone acts where, and "point and shoot". He also corrected one of his slides in class: most aromatase activity is in the Sertoli cells, not the Leydig cells (see Making testosterone). The 4 G's of sexual differentiation His slides frame sex as four layers, the 4 G's, and in class he listed them as four ways to classify sex. Genetic, or genotypic, sex is the chromosomes: XY or XX. Gonadal sex is the gonad: testes or ovaries. Phenotypic, or genital, sex is the external genitalia: a penis or a vagina. Gender is gender identity, each person's internal and individual experience of gender: a sense of being a woman, a man, both, neither, or anywhere along the gender spectrum. It may be the same as or different from the sex assigned at birth. The first three layers are built in order, and each depends on the one before it working. The disorders in this lecture are places where they come apart: defects in a receptor or an enzyme leave a person genetically XY, with testes, and still with female genitalia. How a male fetus is built In an XY fetus the early testes form quickly. From then on, the testis builds the rest of the male with three hormonal signals, and his development slide labels each one. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), from the Sertoli cells, makes the Müllerian ducts regress. Without AMH, the Müllerian ducts would go on to form female internal structures such as the uterus. He called this "an important piece to remember." Testosterone, from the Leydig cells, acts on the Wolffian ducts to build the internal male structures: the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles. Testosterone is high during development. The Leydig cells are driven by LH and by hCG, which the placenta makes in large amounts in early gestation. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is made from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase. DHT forms the external structures, the penis and scrotum; his slide adds the prostate. Without these signals, development follows the default pathway, which is female: female external genitalia and, at puberty, female secondary sex characteristics. Wherever androgens can't act, the external genitalia and the secondary sex characteristics follow this default. That one idea explains both disorders below. One more rule, which holds after birth too: some tissues respond to testosterone itself, and others are much more sensitive to DHT. The DHT tissues express a lot of 5-alpha-reductase, so testosterone that reaches them is converted to DHT there. The Wolffian ducts are testosterone tissue. The penis, scrotum and prostate are DHT tissue. AMH Sertoli cells Müllerian ducts regress Testosterone Leydig cells, driven by hCG and LH Wolffian ducts form the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles DHT Target tissues, by 5-alpha-reductase Penis, scrotum and prostate When a signal fails: two disorders Androgen insensitivity syndrome, also called testicular feminization, is an androgen receptor deficiency, often X-linked: the receptor for testosterone and DHT is mutated or absent. The person is XY, so testes form, but no scrotum develops, so the testes stay inside the body and never descend. The Sertoli cells make AMH, which needs no androgen receptor, so the Müllerian ducts regress: there is no uterus and there are no ovaries. Testosterone and DHT have no working receptor, so the Wolffian ducts regress too. The external genitalia follow the default pathway and are female, with a blind-ended vagina, and the secondary sex characteristics are female: breast development and little body hair. The result is a person who is genetically XY and has testes, but looks female. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency differs by one step. The enzyme is low or absent. The person is XY with testes. AMH works, so there are no Müllerian ducts. Testosterone is made and its receptor works, so the Wolffian ducts develop: internally, the epididymis, seminal vesicles and vas deferens are male. But testosterone can't be converted to DHT, so the external genitalia are female. These children are often raised as girls, and the diagnosis often comes at puberty: testosterone rises, and because testosterone acts on its own, they develop male secondary sex characteristics, such as body hair and muscle mass, which is what brings them in. The fastest way to tell them apart is to ask whether testosterone itself can act. In androgen insensitivity it can't: the Wolffian ducts are gone and puberty is female. In 5-alpha-reductase deficiency it can: the Wolffian ducts are there and puberty brings male changes. In both, AMH works, so neither has a uterus, and in both the external genitalia are female. Cause Androgen receptor mutated or absent (often X-linked) No conversion of testosterone to DHT Karyotype and gonads XY; testes inside the body, never descended XY, testes Müllerian ducts Regressed (AMH works): no uterus or ovaries Absent (AMH works) Wolffian ducts Regressed Developed (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles) External genitalia Female, blind-ended vagina Female At puberty Female: breasts, little body hair Male changes (body hair, muscle mass); often how it's diagnosed What the male reproductive system does His slide lists three major functions: spermatogenesis, sexual performance, and regulation of sexual characteristics and functions through hormones. He spent most of the hour on spermatogenesis and its hormones. The testis Most of each testis is seminiferous tubules, tightly coiled tubules in whose walls sperm develop. The most immature cells sit against the wall of the tubule, and as they mature they move toward the lumen, into which the spermatozoa are finally released. From the tubules, sperm pass to the epididymis, which stores them, and the vas deferens carries them on to the urethra. Between the tubules, in the connective tissue of the interstitium, sit the Leydig cells, which make testosterone; his slide puts this connective tissue at about 20 percent of the testis. The two testes sit in the scrotum, an extension of the abdominal wall. His slide notes add that one testis commonly hangs lower than the other, because the blood vessels on the two sides differ. Sertoli cells, the nurse cells Sertoli cells run through the whole wall of the tubule and wrap around the developing sperm. Their jobs: Nourish and support the developing sperm as they divide and mature. Form tight junctions with one another, creating the blood-testis barrier. The testis is an immune-privileged site: if immune cells got in, they could mount an autoreactive response against the haploid germ cells and damage them. Secrete fluid into the lumen that helps push sperm out of the tubules toward the epididymis. Secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), which binds testosterone and keeps it highly concentrated in the tubules. Testosterone in the testis is higher than in the blood, and the developing sperm depend on that strong signal. Carry out spermiation: they strip the excess cytoplasm as spermatids become spermatozoa and release them into the lumen. His slide notes describe this as a process over several days at the inner edge of the epithelium. Phagocytose defective sperm, secrete inhibin, make aromatase, and, in the fetus, secrete AMH. Sertoli cells are the FSH target: they have a high expression of FSH receptors (Leydig cells have some, but far fewer). FSH binds its receptor, a Gs protein-coupled receptor that activates protein kinase A, or PKA, and the Sertoli cell steps up all its jobs: more nourishment, more ABP, more tight junctions, and inhibin, plus aromatase. Leydig cells, the testosterone makers Leydig cells sit in the interstitium, outside the tubules. Their function is the synthesis of testosterone: "that's their major contribution," he said, "worth remembering." They have a high expression of the LH receptor, which is also a Gs-coupled receptor that activates PKA. PKA phosphorylates the enzymes of testosterone synthesis and turns on the genes for more of them, such as the P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme. Where In the wall of the seminiferous tubule, wrapped around the sperm Interstitium, between the tubules Driven by FSH (Gs, PKA) LH (Gs, PKA) Makes ABP, inhibin, tubular fluid, aromatase (so estradiol); AMH in the fetus Testosterone Other jobs Nourish sperm, blood-testis barrier, spermiation, phagocytose defective sperm Can turn adrenal androgens into testosterone Feeds back on FSH, at the pituitary (inhibin) GnRH and LH (testosterone) Keeping the testes cool Spermatogenesis is temperature sensitive and works best at about 34 degrees Celsius, a few degrees below core body temperature; he gave 34 in class, as his slide does. Three things keep the testes there: The testes sit outside the abdomen, in the scrotum. Two muscles move them. When it is warm, the testes descend farther from the body to cool; he tied this to the cremaster muscle. When it is cold, the dartos muscle contracts, the scrotum tightens, and the testes are pulled closer to the body to stay warm. His slide notes put the rule simply: testicles descend to get cooler and rise to get warmer. The arteries and veins supplying the testis intertwine and exchange heat, from the arteries to the veins, which cools the arterial blood before it reaches the testis. Anatomy texts describe the cremaster as the muscle that lifts the testes when it contracts in the cold, and lets them down when it relaxes. Either way the rule for the exam is the same: warm, the testes hang lower; cold, they're pulled up and the scrotum tightens. Dr. Herr's histology lecture gives about 35 degrees Celsius; for a question on this lecture, use 34. Spermatogenesis He spent most of the lecture here. The cells closest to the tubule wall are the spermatogonia, the least differentiated form; his slide puts them in the outer 2 to 3 layers of the tubule. Spermatogonia keep dividing by mitosis, so new ones are always being made, and some go on to become spermatocytes. The spermatocyte stage is where meiosis happens. A primary spermatocyte completes the first meiotic division and becomes two secondary spermatocytes; the second division turns them into spermatids. No new chromosomes are formed in the second division. So one spermatocyte gives rise to four spermatids, each haploid, with 23 unpaired chromosomes: 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y. In the recording he put each meiotic division one step early (meiosis I forming the primary spermatocyte). The order above, from his slide's diagram and Dr. Herr's histology lecture, is the standard one: primary spermatocyte, meiosis I, secondary spermatocytes, meiosis II, spermatids. A spermatid still looks like an ordinary cell, with a lot of cytoplasm. The Sertoli cells strip the excess cytoplasm away, and the spermatid becomes a spermatozoon, mostly nuclear material, some mitochondria and a flagellum. His slide gives about two months for spermatids to mature into spermatozoa. Dr. Herr's histology lecture gives a different measure: about 74 days for one whole round of spermatogenesis, from spermatogonium to sperm. This lecture's two months, from the slide, is the time the spermatids take to mature. Maturation in the epididymis The spermatozoa released into the tubule are not functional yet: they can't move and can't fertilize. Maturation is completed in the epididymis. About 18 to 24 hours after sperm enter it, signals there (enzymes and growth factors from the epididymis's cells and fluid) let them start to gain motility and the ability to fertilize. His slide adds that they lose cytoplasm and acquire forward motility proteins and acrosomal stabilizing factors. Sperm are also stored in the epididymis, for up to several months. Dr. Herr's histology lecture gives 2 to 12 days for maturation in the epididymis; this lecture's 18 to 24 hours is when the change begins. The structure of a sperm Head: mostly the nuclear region, with the genetic material that fertilizes the ovum. Acrosome: the cap at the very top of the head, a specialized vacuole formed from the Golgi apparatus. It holds hyaluronidase and proteolytic enzymes that let the sperm penetrate the layers that protect the egg (more on those layers in L16 and L17). Midpiece, or body: packed with mitochondria, which make the energy that keeps the flagellum moving. Tail: a flagellum whose movement gives the sperm its motility. Making testosterone Testosterone is a steroid hormone: the Leydig cells make it from cholesterol in response to LH. LH stimulates the expression and activity of cholesterol desmolase, the P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme, the key regulated step; it's the same step ACTH controls in the adrenal cortex. His slide calls it the rate-limiting step. The weak adrenal androgens, DHEA and androstenedione, can also be funneled into this pathway, so the Leydig cells can turn them into testosterone (and in women, they feed the female sex hormones, L16). Once testosterone is made, two enzymes take it in different directions: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in the tissues that are more sensitive to DHT, which express a lot of the enzyme. Aromatase, also called estrogen synthase, converts testosterone into estradiol and androstenedione into estrone; estrone is the main source of estrogen after menopause (L16). FSH turns aromatase up. Where aromatase sits: mostly in the Sertoli cells, from fetal development onward. His slide says that in pubertal and adult males the activity resides in the Leydig cells; in class he called that "an old way of thinking" and told the class to cross it out: "Sertoli cells are pretty much the predominant" source, and Leydig cells have some. For the exam, answer Sertoli cells. Estrogen has a real, if small, role in men, at levels far below those in women. The Sertoli cells' aromatase turns some of the testosterone that reaches the tubule into estradiol. Some of that estradiol goes into the blood and supports tissues outside the testes. Some goes back to the Leydig cells and stimulates their protein synthesis; estradiol promotes protein synthesis and anabolic pathways in many target tissues. P450 side-chain cleavage (cholesterol desmolase) First step from cholesterol Rate-limiting; turned on by LH, as ACTH does in the adrenal 5-alpha-reductase Testosterone to DHT In DHT tissues: penis, scrotum, prostate Aromatase (estrogen synthase) Testosterone to estradiol; androstenedione to estrone Mostly Sertoli cells (FSH), from fetal life on; some in Leydig Hormonal control: the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GnRH, which stimulates the gonadotropes of the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH. Both travel in the blood to the testes, where each acts mainly on one cell type. LH binds mainly the Leydig cells, which make testosterone. FSH binds mainly the Sertoli cells, which support spermatogenesis and make ABP and inhibin. Testosterone also moves into the tubules and acts on the Sertoli cells, speeding spermatogenesis; ABP keeps it concentrated there. Two hormones close the loop by negative feedback, and they act in different places: Testosterone acts at both levels: it turns off GnRH at the hypothalamus and, at the anterior pituitary, mainly LH. Inhibin, from the Sertoli cells, acts only at the anterior pituitary, where it turns off FSH, not LH. Asked in class, he was clear that inhibin doesn't feed back to the hypothalamus. (Testosterone's brake on GnRH lowers FSH too, indirectly.) When serum testosterone falls, GnRH and LH secretion rise; when it rises, they fall. These loops keep serum testosterone within a narrow range. His slide adds a point about timing: GnRH, and so LH, must be released in pulses to maintain normal testosterone production. Continuous GnRH does the opposite of what you might expect: it decreases LH secretion, and therefore decreases testosterone. The two-cell, two-gonadotropin model His summary slide puts the pieces together: two cells, each run by its own gonadotropin through a Gs receptor and PKA. The Leydig cell answers to LH and makes testosterone. The Sertoli cell answers to FSH and makes inhibin, ABP, and the growth factors and proteins that nourish the maturing sperm, and it phagocytoses defective sperm. Testosterone passes from the Leydig cells into the tubule, where the developing sperm use it, and the Sertoli cells' aromatase turns some of it into estradiol, which goes to the blood and back to the Leydig cells. Reading a hormone pattern The feedback rules let you locate a problem from three numbers: testosterone, LH and FSH. The hub's case questions apply them this way. Failing testes: testosterone is low, and with the brake off, LH and FSH are high. Failing pituitary: LH and FSH are low, so testosterone is low too. Testosterone taken from outside, as in anabolic steroid use: blood testosterone is high, and it suppresses GnRH and LH, so LH and FSH are low. With the testes no longer stimulated, the high testosterone inside the testis that spermatogenesis needs is lost, and the sperm count falls even though blood testosterone is high. Damaged tubules, healthy Leydig cells: inhibin falls, so FSH rises on its own, while LH and testosterone stay normal. Continuous GnRH: LH falls, and testosterone falls with it. Failing testes Low High High Failing pituitary Low Low Low Testosterone injections High Low Low Damaged tubules only (low inhibin) Normal Normal High Continuous GnRH Low Low Not on the slides Testosterone across life His slide traces testosterone with age, and he walked through it. Testosterone is high during gestation, building the male structures; it peaks again soon after birth; then it goes quiet through childhood. It surges at puberty and stays fairly steady through adulthood: it has peaks and valleys, but it isn't cyclic the way the female hormones are. In old age it declines. That decline is multifactorial and still not fully understood: sometimes the Leydig cells stop responding to LH as they should, sometimes the problem is at the hypothalamus. His slide notes call the gradual decline late-onset hypogonadism, or age-related low testosterone. The accessory glands and semen Three accessory glands, the seminal vesicles, the prostate and the bulbourethral glands, secrete the seminal fluid, and their secretions are added to the sperm as they pass through the vas deferens and urethra. Semen, the ejaculate, is sperm plus seminal fluid. Most of what the glands add supports sperm survival and movement in the female reproductive tract. Seminal vesicles: secretory glands that make about 60 to 70 percent of the seminal fluid (his slide says 50 to 80; Dr. Herr's histology lecture, about 70). Their fluid has fructose, which the sperm metabolize for the energy to swim, citric acid and other nutrients. It has prostaglandins, which, once the semen is in the female reproductive tract, stimulate contractions of the tract that help the sperm move. And it has fibrinogen and other clotting factors: soon after ejaculation the semen clots, which keeps the sperm in the female tract longer. The fluid is somewhat alkaline. During ejaculation the seminal vesicle empties into the ejaculatory duct. Prostate: about the size of a walnut, below the bladder, surrounding the urethra. It makes about 20 to 30 percent of the seminal fluid, a thin, milky fluid with citrate, phosphate and calcium, which support the sperm's metabolism, movement and survival, and alkaline fluid that neutralizes the acidic environment the sperm enter. It also makes prostate-specific antigen, PSA, which is sometimes measured to check the prostate's health. PSA is an enzyme, a serine protease: it breaks down the semen clot over time, so the sperm can move on toward the fallopian tubes. His slide also lists a clotting enzyme and profibrinolysin in prostatic fluid. Bulbourethral glands, or Cowper's glands: mostly for lubrication. Their clear, thick mucus comes before ejaculation, and it is alkaline, so it neutralizes the acidic pH of the urethra; it is thought to flush out the urethra before the semen comes. Seminal vesicles Fructose, citric acid, prostaglandins, fibrinogen 60 to 70 percent of the fluid; energy for sperm; contractions of the female tract; the clot that holds sperm there Prostate Thin, milky fluid: citrate, phosphate, calcium; PSA 20 to 30 percent; neutralizes acidity; PSA breaks down the clot Bulbourethral (Cowper's) Clear, thick mucus, before ejaculation Lubricates and neutralizes the urethra The male sexual act: point and shoot The male sexual response is controlled by both divisions of the autonomic nervous system. Everything leading up to ejaculation, the erection and the lubrication, is parasympathetic; the climax, emission and ejaculation, is sympathetic. His mnemonic is "Point and Shoot": P for point, parasympathetic; S for shoot, sympathetic. "It's crude, but you'll remember it." Erection, the "point": parasympathetic nerves, acting through nitric oxide. Lubrication: also parasympathetic. Emission and ejaculation, the "shoot": sympathetic. The physiology of erection The penis is mostly spongy, cavernous connective tissue: the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum. The vessels to remember are the cavernosal arteries, which drive the erection. During sexual arousal the parasympathetic nerves fire, and their postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine and nitric oxide. Nitric oxide is the key: it dilates the cavernosal arteries, more blood flows into the spongy tissue, and the tissue engorges. The engorged tissue then compresses the veins that drain it, so the blood can't drain out, and the result is an erection. At the molecular level, nitric oxide activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which converts GTP into cyclic GMP, or cGMP. As cGMP rises, the arterial smooth muscle relaxes, the vessels dilate, and everything above follows. cGMP is normally broken down quickly by phosphodiesterase type 5, PDE5, which ends the signal. The path of sperm Sperm are formed in the seminiferous tubules with the support of Sertoli cells. They move into the epididymis, where they mature and are stored, for up to several months. During ejaculation, driven by the sympathetic nervous system, sperm move from the epididymis through the vas deferens and empty into the urethra, mixing all the while with the secretions of the accessory glands. Treating erectile dysfunction: sildenafil Drugs for erectile dysfunction use this same pathway. Sildenafil (Viagra) inhibits PDE5, the enzyme that degrades cGMP. With PDE5 blocked, cGMP stays high for longer, the arterial smooth muscle keeps relaxing, and the erection is maintained. His slide adds that on its own sildenafil has no direct relaxant effect on the corpus cavernosum: it enhances the effect of nitric oxide, so it works only when sexual stimulation releases NO. Without NO there is no cGMP for it to protect. If you read the posted slides: the speaker notes under the first two development slides describe the adrenal gland. They appear to be left over from another deck and aren't part of this lecture.
